paragraphs: Here's what this riddle teaches, friend: the vine had everything. Good soil, abundant waters, a setup to bear fruit and become a splendid vine (Ezekiel 17:8). And it still reached for another eagle instead of trusting the ground it was planted in. Then God explains it, and the king who broke his covenant with Babylon had done the same thing, sending to Egypt for horses and a large army (Ezekiel 17:15).

God asks, 'Can he break a covenant and yet escape?' (Ezekiel 17:15). Then He calls the oath that king despised and the covenant that he broke His OWN (Ezekiel 17:19). So this isn't just a story about politics, baker. It's about what happens when someone gives his hand in pledge and then breaks his word (Ezekiel 17:18), and God calls that treason against Him (Ezekiel 17:20).

But don't walk away discouraged, because the passage doesn't end on the withered vine. God Himself says He will take a tender sprig, plant it on the mountain heights of Israel, and it will become a majestic cedar where birds of every kind find shelter (Ezekiel 17:22-23). He brings the tall tree down and makes the low tree tall, and then says, 'I, the LORD, have spoken, and I have done it.' (Ezekiel 17:24). Take it from a stamper who got pulled out of a junk drawer: when your own reaching leaves you withered, God's promise is the one thing that still stands.
